questions.title: JavaScript Frontend Interview Overview
questions.direct_answer: A JavaScript frontend interview evaluates your understanding of JavaScript's core language mechanics (closures, the event loop, prototypes, async) and the framework you work in (React/Angular/Vue), at the level the role demands. It exists because JavaScript is unlike most languages — single-threaded with an event loop, prototype-based, with closures that underpin every async pattern — and a frontend engineer who memorizes framework APIs but doesn't understand these mechanics cannot debug real UIs when they break. The interview verifies that depth before hiring you to build user-facing software.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what a JS interview uniquely tests — the event loop, closures, prototypes, async/promise mechanics, and the framework's mental model — not just framework API memorization.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing React/Angular APIs without explaining the event loop, closures, or why `this` behaves as it does — missing that the interview tests the language mechanics the framework sits on.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame the JS interview as testing language mechanics (event loop, closures, prototypes, async) plus the framework's mental model — the mechanics are what let you debug when the framework's abstractions leak.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: A JavaScript frontend interview evaluates your understanding of JavaScript's core language mechanics and the framework you work in, at the level the role demands. It exists because JavaScript is unlike most languages — single-threaded with an event loop, prototype-based, with closures that underpin every async pattern — and an engineer who memorizes framework APIs but doesn't understand these mechanics cannot debug real UIs when they break. The interview verifies that depth before hiring you to build user-facing software. It typically spans the language core (closures, the event loop, prototypes, this, async/await), the framework (React/Angular/Vue components, state, rendering), the DOM and browser APIs, and frontend engineering (performance, accessibility, testing).

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas a JS interview tests: (1) the event loop — JS is single-threaded; the call stack, the microtask queue (promises), and the macrotask queue (setTimeout, I/O) determine execution order, and interviewers love asking what runs first; (2) closures — a function retains access to its lexical scope; this underpins modules, currying, and every React hook (useState is a closure over state); (3) prototypes and this — JS is prototype-based; `this` is determined by the call site, and the prototype chain drives inheritance; (4) async — promises, async/await, and the microtask queue; (5) the framework's mental model — React's reconciliation/virtual DOM, Angular's change detection; (6) the DOM and browser APIs; (7) frontend engineering — performance (Core Web Vitals), accessibility, testing.

sections.title: JS Interview: Language Mechanics vs Framework APIs
The event loop and a closure — the two most-tested mechanics
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is framework fluency versus language depth: a candidate can build features by copying React/Angular patterns but cannot debug them when they break (stale closures, re-render storms, event-loop starvation) without the underlying mechanics — the interview tests both. A second tension: JS has grown (ES6+, TypeScript, async/await) but its core (event loop, prototypes, this) is unchanged and still tested; don't confuse modern syntax with changed mechanics. The third: frontend interviews also weigh engineering breadth (performance, accessibility, testing) that pure algorithm rounds miss.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A JS interview tests language mechanics (event loop, closures, prototypes, this, async) AND the framework's mental model — not just framework APIs.
The event loop: JS is single-threaded; microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (setTimeout) — predict execution order.
Closures underpin modules, currying, and every React hook (useState is a closure over state); stale closures are a common bug.
JS is prototype-based; `this` is determined by the call site — know new/bind/call/apply and the prototype chain.
Framework depth matters (React reconciliation, Angular change detection) — but it sits on top of the language mechanics, which is what you debug when abstractions leak.
Frontend interviews also test engineering breadth: performance (Core Web Vitals), accessibility, and testing.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A JavaScript frontend interview evaluates your command of the language's core mechanics — the event loop, closures, prototypes, this, and async — plus the framework you work in, at the level the role demands. It exists because JavaScript is unlike most languages: it's single-threaded with an event loop, prototype-based, and closures underpin every async pattern, so an engineer who memorizes React or Angular APIs but doesn't understand these mechanics can't debug real UIs when they break. The two most-tested mechanics are the event loop, where microtasks like promises run before macrotasks like setTimeout and interviewers love asking what runs first; and closures, where a function retains its lexical scope, which underpins modules, currying, and every React hook — useState is a closure over state, and stale closures are a common bug. I also anchor on prototypes and this, which is determined by the call site and drives OO in JS, and on the framework's mental model, like React's reconciliation or Angular's change detection. The honest tension is framework fluency versus language depth: you can build features by copying patterns, but you can't debug them when they break without the mechanics, so the interview tests both. And frontend interviews also weigh engineering breadth — performance like Core Web Vitals, accessibility, and testing — that pure algorithm rounds miss.

questions.title: React Reconciliation & Virtual DOM
questions.question: How does React's reconciliation algorithm work, and what is the Virtual DOM's role in it?

sections.content: This is a foundational question Meta and Netflix love. They want you to explain the VDOM as a lightweight representation, the diffing algorithm (O(n) heuristics), and why keys matter. A strong answer connects this to practical performance decisions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Virtual DOM is a programming model, not a speed hack** — it makes complex UIs manageable with acceptable performance, not always faster than direct DOM
- **Two O(n) heuristics** — different element types = full subtree rebuild; `key` prop identifies stable list elements across renders
- **Keys must be stable and unique** — array index keys cause unnecessary remounts on reorder/filter; use `item.id` instead
- **React Fiber makes rendering interruptible** — high-priority updates (user typing) can preempt low-priority ones (data fetching) via `useTransition`
- **Batching in React 18** — all state updates are batched automatically, including in async callbacks, reducing VDOM comparisons

The Virtual DOM is React's lightweight JavaScript representation of the actual DOM tree. When state changes, React builds a new VDOM tree and compares it with the previous one — this is reconciliation. The diff algorithm then figures out the minimal set of real DOM operations needed to bring the UI in sync.

React's diffing uses two key heuristics to stay O(n) instead of O(n³): first, elements of different types produce completely different trees (React won't try to reuse a `<div>` as an `<input>`). Second, keys tell React which list items are the same across renders, enabling it to reorder rather than recreate.

In practice, this means: mismatched element types cause full subtree remounts (expensive), missing or unstable keys in lists cause unnecessary remounts (the classic performance bug), and React batches multiple state updates into a single re-render to minimize VDOM comparisons.

- **Keys must be stable and unique** — don't use `Math.random()` or array indices for mutable lists
- **Component type changes = full remount** — putting a component inside a conditional can cause this unexpectedly
- **`React.memo()`** prevents re-render if props haven't changed — use for pure components that render frequently
- **`useTransition` and `useDeferredValue`** — mark updates as non-urgent to keep UI responsive
- **Batching in React 18** — all state updates are batched automatically, including in async callbacks

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
React stores hook state in a linked list attached to the component's fiber node.

Each hook call is identified purely by its position in the call order — not by a name or key.

On the first render, React initializes the list. On subsequent renders, it reads from the list in the same order, matching each `useState` call to its stored state value. If you put a hook inside an `if` statement or loop, the order can change between renders. The hook that used to be at position 2 might now be at position 1, and React reads the wrong state for it.

Memorizing React/Angular APIs without explaining the event loop, closures, or why `this` behaves as it does — missing that the interview tests the language mechanics the framework sits on.

You have a list of 10,000 items rendered in a React component. A state update causes all 10,000 to re-render even though only 5 changed. What are three strategies to fix this, and when would you choose each?

questions.question: What is React Fiber and how does it improve over the old reconciler?
questions.quickAnswer: Fiber is React's rewrite of reconciliation into an interruptible work loop. Allows prioritization, time-slicing, and Concurrent features like Suspense and useTransition.

questions.question: When does React.memo not help?
questions.quickAnswer: When props are objects/functions created inline — they get new references every render. Combine with useMemo/useCallback to stabilize references.

questions.title: React Hooks — Rules and Internals
questions.question: Why must React hooks be called in the same order every render, and what happens internally if you break this rule?

sections.content: A question that separates engineers who use hooks from those who understand them. The interviewer wants to hear about the linked list of hook state, why order matters, and what practical rules this creates.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hooks are identified by call order, not name** — React walks a linked list of hook slots on every render; position is the only identifier
- **Conditional hooks corrupt state** — skipping a hook shifts all subsequent slots; React reads the wrong stored value, causing silent data corruption
- **Conditional logic goes inside hooks** — `useEffect(() => { if (x) { ... } })` is correct; `if (x) { useEffect(...) }` breaks the rules
- **Stale closures are the #1 useEffect bug** — missing dependencies cause the effect to capture an old value; the exhaustive-deps lint rule catches this
- **Custom hooks are just functions** — they share the caller's linked list; `useUserData` is convention, not magic

React stores hook state in a linked list attached to the component's fiber node. Each hook call is identified purely by its position in the call order — not by a name or key. On the first render, React initializes the list. On subsequent renders, it reads from the list in the same order, matching each `useState` call to its stored state value.

If you put a hook inside an `if` statement or loop, the order can change between renders. The hook that used to be at position 2 might now be at position 1, and React reads the wrong state for it. This corrupts state and causes completely unpredictable bugs — which is exactly why the linter enforces the two rules: only call hooks at the top level, only call them in React functions.

The practical implication: conditional logic goes inside the hook, not around it. You can't use early returns before hooks.

- **Rules of Hooks are not arbitrary** — they directly reflect the linked list implementation
- **eslint-plugin-react-hooks** — install this; it catches violations at development time
- **Cleanup functions in useEffect** — always return cleanup for subscriptions, timers, and fetch cancellation
- **Stale closures** — the #1 `useEffect` bug: forgetting to add a dependency causes the closure to capture an old value
- **`useRef` for mutable values** — doesn't trigger re-render; good for interval IDs, previous values, DOM refs

questions.title: State Management Patterns
questions.question: When would you use local state, Context, Redux, Zustand, or React Query for state management — and what are the trade-offs?

sections.content: They want a nuanced answer that doesn't default to 'Redux for everything' or 'Context is fine'. The key insight: server state and client state are different problems requiring different tools.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Server state ≠ client state** — API data needs caching/invalidation (React Query/SWR); UI state needs synchronous reads (useState/Zustand)
- **Context causes full consumer re-renders** — every component consuming the context re-renders on any value change, even for unchanged fields
- **Zustand selectors prevent re-render storms** — `useStore(s => s.count)` only re-renders when `count` changes, unlike Context
- **useReducer for complex transitions** — when next state depends on multiple fields or you want named actions, useReducer is cleaner than chained setters
- **Redux for large teams with strict needs** — time-travel debugging and action logging justify the boilerplate; rarely the right first choice for new projects

The biggest conceptual shift in modern React state management is separating server state from client state. Server state (data fetched from an API) has caching, invalidation, background refetching, and loading concerns. Client state (UI state like modal open/closed, selected tab) is synchronous and always current.

For server state: React Query or SWR. These handle caching, deduplication, background updates, and stale-while-revalidate automatically — problems that Redux + thunks handle poorly. For client state: local `useState` for component-scoped state, Context for low-frequency global state (theme, auth), and Zustand or Jotai for complex global client state that would cause Context re-render storms.

Redux is the right choice for very large teams with complex state mutations that need time-travel debugging, strict action logging, or a large existing Redux codebase. It's rarely the right first choice for a new project.

- **Server state ≠ client state** — React Query for APIs, Zustand for UI state
- **Context causes re-renders** — every consumer re-renders when value changes, even if they don't use the changed part
- **Zustand selectors** — `useStore(state => state.count)` only re-renders when `count` changes, not on any store change
- **React Query v5** (`@tanstack/react-query`) — `cacheTime` renamed to `gcTime`
- **DevTools for all of them** — React Query DevTools, Redux DevTools, Zustand's built-in logging
